editorNote: IBM’s two-year-old personal computer now casts the industry’s longest shadow, while home-machine makers regroup for Christmas.
morningLine: Big Blue defines the PC standard, Radio Shack refreshes the Color Computer, and holiday buyers hunt scarce drives and machines.

lead.headline: Big Blue Paints the Personal-Computer Standard
lead.dek: IBM captures the business desktop as software houses and add-on makers rally around its open specifications.
body: Only two years after entering personal computers, IBM has seized roughly 40 percent of the $2,000-to-$5,000 desktop market. That share tells only part of the story: the IBM PC has become the reference point against which business buyers, software publishers and would-be compatible makers now measure their plans.

More than 900 of the roughly 1,200 software companies operating before the PC appeared are now writing for IBM’s machine, according to this week’s industry assessment. New PC packages are arriving at a pace of about 50 each month, turning compatibility into a powerful sales argument for offices that want a broad catalog rather than a solitary machine.

IBM helped create that surrounding market by publishing technical specifications that independent manufacturers could study. Expansion boards, peripherals and compatible systems have multiplied, making the PC less a sealed product than the center of an increasingly busy commercial ecosystem.

The momentum also raises the stakes for every rival. Apple retains a devoted base and home computers compete fiercely below $1,000, but business software is gathering around Big Blue. At Christmas 1983, the most important feature of IBM’s PC may be the standard forming beyond the blue badge.

stories.headline: Home-Computer Price War Eases After a Savage 1983
body: The holiday market is emerging from a price war that pushed Texas Instruments out of home computers and left Atari nursing heavy losses. Commodore 64 street prices below $200 and VIC-20 prices below $100 delighted buyers, but the cuts punished manufacturers and dealers alike.

IBM’s PCjr, priced from roughly $700 to $1,300, has given surviving makers room to stop racing toward the bottom. Atari and Coleco raised prices after its unveiling, while shortages of components and popular disk drives put a practical floor beneath further holiday markdowns.

stories.headline: Radio Shack Refreshes the Color Computer Line
body: Radio Shack is answering the crowded holiday shelves with a 64K Extended BASIC Color Computer at $399.95 and two Color Computer 2 models at $239.95 and $319.95. All arrive with full-stroke keyboards, a welcome upgrade for buyers who intend to type more than game commands.

The 64K model can use its full memory with the $399.95 Color 2 Disk Kit and $69.95 OS-9 operating system, and can support as many as four drives. The less expensive Color Computer 2 machines retain cassette storage, keeping a lower-priced door open for first-time owners.

stories.headline: Lotus 1-2-3 Overtakes the Spreadsheet Pioneer
body: Lotus 1-2-3 is rapidly displacing VisiCalc as the business spreadsheet of choice. Its $495 package combines calculation, graphics and limited filing and writing tools, offering office buyers a coordinated suite rather than a single electronic ledger.

VisiCalc, once $350, has fallen to $250, but software prices remain tied to the costly work of development and support. Contemporary estimates place development of a major new program between $200,000 and $500,000, explaining why the strongest business titles resist the hardware market’s price war.

stories.headline: Christmas Computer Boom Meets Empty Shelves
body: The promised “Christmas of the Computer” has arrived unevenly. Commodore was shipping at enormous volume, yet Commodore 64 machines and disk drives could still be scarce, while Coleco’s Adam missed its August debut and reached FCC approval only in October.

Atari’s 600XL and 800XL were expected for Christmas, but delayed machines and canceled dealer orders made selection depend as much on availability as specifications. Families shopping this week may find that the computer in the advertisement is not the computer on the counter.
